title: Circuit components — diodes, LDRs and thermistors
examTip: I-V graphs are favourite exam targets. Know the shape for a fixed resistor, a diode and a filament lamp. Be ready to explain each shape in terms of resistance.
introTips: Before you read, sketch the I-V graph for a fixed resistor and for a diode. Then check if you were right.
Make flashcards for the LDR and thermistor. What happens to resistance when the physical quantity increases?
Circuit symbols come up in every paper. Practise drawing them from memory.
intro: Why does your phone charger get warm but barely flicker the lights? Why do street lamps switch on by themselves at dusk? The answer is how different components respond to the conditions around them. Some change their resistance with light. Some change it with heat. Some only let current through in one direction. These components are the base of every electronic device you have ever used.

basics.text: Current is how much electric charge flows past a point each second. Think of cars passing under a bridge: more cars each second is a bigger flow. It is measured in amperes (A), often called amps.
Potential difference is the push that makes charge move round a circuit. A cell or battery gives it. It is measured in volts (V), and a bigger number means a bigger push.

Resistance is how hard it is for current to get through something. It is like a narrow, crowded corridor that slows people down. More resistance means less current for the same push. It is measured in ohms (Ω).

basics.idea: The two axes of a graph
basics.text: A graph has a line across the bottom, called the x-axis. The line up the side is the y-axis. Each one shows a quantity you measured. Each point on the graph is one pair of readings.
The origin is the corner of a graph where both axes start at zero. A line "through the origin" starts from that corner. It means that when one quantity is zero, so is the other.
Two quantities are directly proportional when doubling one doubles the other. Apples are like this: twice as many apples cost twice as much. On a graph this is a straight line through the origin.
Light intensity means how bright the light is. A sunny window has a high light intensity. A dark cupboard has a low one.

keyPoints.heading: Fixed resistors and variable resistors
keyPoints.content: A fixed resistor has a constant resistance at a constant temperature. For some resistors, the value of R stays constant. In others, it changes as the current changes. The resistance of lamps, diodes, thermistors and LDRs is not constant. It changes with the current through them. The equation V = IR links potential difference, current and resistance for any component. Here V is potential difference (volts, V), I is current (amps, A) and R is resistance (ohms, Ω). For an ohmic conductor at a constant temperature, the current is directly proportional to the potential difference. A variable resistor (also called a rheostat) lets you change the resistance by hand. You slide a contact along a resistive wire or track. They are used in dimmer switches, volume controls and lab experiments to control current. Take an I-V graph for an ohmic conductor (a fixed resistor at constant temperature). Current goes on the y-axis and potential difference on the x-axis. You get a straight line through the origin. The steeper the line, the lower the resistance. Doubling the resistance halves the gradient. Worked example: R = 10 Ω, V = 5 V → I = V ÷ R = 5 ÷ 10 = 0.5 A.
writeBullets: Fixed resistor — constant resistance at a constant temperature
Variable resistor (rheostat) — the user can change the resistance by hand
V = IR — links potential difference, current and resistance for any component
Ohmic conductor — at constant temperature, current is directly proportional to potential difference
Lamps, diodes, thermistors and LDRs — resistance is not constant. It changes with the current
I-V graph: straight line through the origin. Constant gradient = constant resistance
Steeper gradient on I-V graph → lower resistance (more current per volt)
Units: V in volts, I in amps, R in ohms

keyTerms.def: A component whose resistance stays constant at constant temperature — produces a straight-line I-V graph through the origin.
A resistor whose resistance can be changed manually, used to control current in a circuit.
The opposition to current flow; measured in ohms (Ω). R = V ÷ I.

keyPoints.memTip: Straight line = straight behaviour = fixed resistor. If the graph curves, something is changing.
keyPoints.tutor_note: It is easy to mix up gradient and resistance. A steeper gradient means MORE current for the same potential difference. So it means LOWER resistance.

keyPoints.heading: Diodes
keyPoints.content: A diode is a component that only lets current flow in one direction, the forward direction. In the reverse direction, the diode has a very high resistance. So only a very small current flows. On an I-V graph, the diode shows a flat line near zero for negative potential differences. In the forward direction, the current rises steeply. The circuit symbol is a triangle pointing the way current flows. A vertical bar blocks flow the other way. An LED (light-emitting diode) is a diode that gives out light when current flows forwards. LEDs are used in TVs, phone screens, traffic lights and energy-efficient lighting.
writeBullets: Diode — lets current flow forwards only. In the reverse direction, very high resistance and a very small current
I-V graph — flat for negative V, then a steep rise in the forward direction
LED — gives out light when forward current flows. Used in energy-efficient lighting
Circuit symbol — triangle + bar. The triangle points the way current flows

keyTerms.def: A component that allows current to flow in one direction only, with very high resistance in the reverse direction.
Light-emitting diode — a diode that releases light energy when current flows through it in the forward direction.

keyPoints.memTip: The triangle in the symbol points the way current can go. It is like an arrow saying 'this way only'.
keyPoints.tutor_note: The flat part of the diode I-V graph is often misread. It is not zero resistance. It is extremely high resistance, so the current is negligible.

keyPoints.heading: Light-Dependent Resistors (LDRs)
keyPoints.content: An LDR (light-dependent resistor) is a component whose resistance decreases as light intensity increases. In the dark, its resistance is very high, and can be hundreds of kΩ. In bright light, its resistance can drop to just a few hundred ohms. Uses: - automatic street lights: when it gets dark, the LDR's resistance rises and the circuit switches the light on - burglar alarms: breaking a light beam changes the LDR's resistance, which sets off the alarm - camera exposure meters and garden solar lights Graph shape: resistance on the y-axis, light intensity on the x-axis → a downward curve (not a straight line).
writeBullets: LDR — resistance decreases as light intensity increases
Dark — very high resistance (hundreds of kΩ). Bright light — low resistance (hundreds of Ω)
Used to switch street lights on when it gets dark, and in burglar alarms and camera exposure meters
Graph: resistance vs light intensity is a downward curve

keyTerms.def: Light-dependent resistor — a component whose resistance decreases as light intensity increases.

keyPoints.memTip: More light → less resistance → more current. Think of a crowd and doors. More light opens more doors, so it is easier to get through.
keyPoints.tutor_note: LDRs and thermistors are easy to mix up. In both, more of the quantity means less resistance. But the trigger is different. An LDR responds to light. A thermistor responds to temperature.

keyPoints.heading: Thermistors
keyPoints.content: A thermistor is a component whose resistance decreases as temperature increases. The hotter it gets, the lower its resistance. At low temperatures, its resistance is high. Worked example: at 20°C a thermistor might have R = 5000 Ω. At 100°C it might fall to 200 Ω. Uses: thermostats (central heating) and fire alarms. Also temperature sensors in car engines and medical devices, and smart home temperature controls. In a thermostat, the thermistor's resistance falls as the room warms up. The circuit uses this change to switch the heating off. Key rule: for an LDR, resistance decreases as light intensity increases. For a thermistor, resistance decreases as temperature increases.
writeBullets: Thermistor — resistance decreases as temperature increases
At low temperatures: high resistance. At high temperatures: low resistance
Used in thermostats, fire alarms and engine temperature sensors
Both LDR and thermistor: more of the physical quantity → less resistance
Graph: resistance vs temperature is a downward curve (not a straight line)

keyTerms.def: A temperature-sensitive resistor whose resistance decreases as temperature increases.

keyPoints.memTip: Thermistor: hot → low resistance. Cold → high resistance.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Common exam question: describe the shape of a thermistor's resistance-temperature graph. Say that resistance decreases as temperature increases, and that the graph is a curve.

0.question: A fixed resistor has V = 12 V and I = 0.4 A. What is its resistance?
0.correctFeedback: Correct! R = V ÷ I = 12 ÷ 0.4 = 30 Ω. Always check your units. Volts and amps give ohms.
0.wrongFeedback: Use R = V ÷ I. Divide 12 V by 0.4 A to get 30 Ω. Don't multiply or add. R = V ÷ I is a division.

1.question: On an I-V graph for a diode, what does the flat line at negative potential differences show?
options: The diode has very high resistance, and almost no current flows in the reverse direction
The diode allows equal current in both directions
1.correctFeedback: Spot on. In the reverse direction the diode has a very high resistance. The flat line shows that only a very small current flows, even as the potential difference grows more negative.
1.wrongFeedback: The flat line does NOT mean zero resistance. It means very high resistance, so the tiny current that does flow is negligible. The diode is blocking current in the reverse direction.

2.question: An LDR is moved from a bright room into a dark cupboard. What happens to its resistance?
2.correctFeedback: Exactly right. In the dark, an LDR's resistance increases a lot. So it is harder for current to flow.
2.wrongFeedback: Remember: for an LDR, MORE light = LESS resistance. So less light (a dark cupboard) means HIGHER resistance.

3.question: A thermostat uses a thermistor. The room gets warmer. What happens to the thermistor's resistance?
3.correctFeedback: Correct. A thermistor's resistance decreases as temperature increases. The thermostat uses this change to switch the heating.
3.wrongFeedback: A thermistor's resistance decreases as temperature increases. So when the room warms up, its resistance goes down.

commonMistakes: Mixing up the gradient of an I-V graph with resistance. A steeper line means lower resistance (more current per volt), not higher.
Thinking a diode has zero resistance in the reverse direction. It has very HIGH resistance. So only a very small current flows.
Mixing up the LDR and thermistor. An LDR responds to light. A thermistor responds to temperature. Both drop in resistance as their quantity increases.
Forgetting that an LED is a type of diode. So it only conducts in the forward direction. It will not light up if it is connected the wrong way round.
examTips: When describing an LDR or thermistor, always say what happens to resistance as light intensity or temperature increases.
For I-V graph questions, describe the shape exactly. For example: 'straight line through the origin', 'curve that gets less steep', or 'flat then sudden steep rise'. Vague answers lose marks.
For circuit questions, write down V = IR first and start from there. Most electricity questions link back to it.
revisionCardBullets: Fixed resistor: constant resistance at constant temperature. Its I-V graph is a straight line through the origin
Variable resistor (rheostat): resistance changed by hand. Used in dimmer switches
V = IR: potential difference = current × resistance
Diode: current in one direction only. Very high resistance in the reverse direction
LED: a diode that gives out light. Used in screens, traffic lights and energy-efficient bulbs
I-V graph for a diode: flat for negative V, steep rise in the forward direction
Resistance of lamps, diodes, thermistors and LDRs is not constant. It changes with the current
LDR uses: automatic street lights, burglar alarms, camera meters
Thermistor uses: thermostats, fire alarms, engine and medical temperature sensors
